The coronavirus outbreak has harmed communities and disrupted economic activity in many countries, including the United States. Consistent with the credit-channel literature, tighter financial conditions can amplify downturns by raising external finance premia and depressing inventories and fixed investment (Oliner and Rudebusch 1996; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994; Gertler and Gilchrist 1994). Against these headwinds, the FOMC’s rapid move to the effective lower bound, large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, and expanded repo and swap lines reflect countercyclical policy designed to stabilize output and anchor inflation expectations when market-based inflation compensation falls (Romer and Romer; McCallum and Nelson 1999; Svensson on inflation-forecast targeting; Sims on monetary policy shocks). Net assessment: near-term sentiment remains negative due to the shock, but strong policy action mitigates downside risks relative to an unchanged-policy counterfactual.
